content: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant with a distinct mechanism of action and is widely used in clinical practice. This review aimed to evaluate its efficacy and acceptability compared to other antidepressants during the acute-phase treatment of major depressive disorder in adults. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared mirtazapine to other antidepressants. A total of 29 RCTs involving 4,974 participants were analyzed. Most studies followed participants for six weeks in outpatient settings, but the risk of bias was often inadequately reported. When compared to tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) in 10 trials with 1,553 participants, there was no significant difference in treatment response at two weeks (odds ratio [OR] 0.85, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64 to 1.13) or at the end of the acute-phase treatment (6 to 12 weeks) (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.10). In comparison to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) in 12 trials with 2,626 participants, mirtazapine demonstrated significantly greater efficacy at two weeks (OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.30 to 1.88) and at the end of the acute-phase treatment (OR 1.19, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.39). When compared to serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), specifically venlafaxine, in two trials with 415 participants, mirtazapine was significantly more effective at two weeks (OR 2.29, 95% CI 1.45 to 3.59) and at the end of the acute-phase treatment (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.25). Regarding dropout rates, there was no significant difference between mirtazapine and other antidepressants. However, mirtazapine was associated with a unique adverse event profile. It was more likely to cause weight gain, increased appetite, and somnolence compared to SSRIs, but it was less likely to cause nausea, vomiting, or sexual dysfunction. In conclusion, mirtazapine showed some statistically significant and potentially clinically meaningful differences compared to other antidepressants in the acute-phase treatment of major depression. It appears to have a faster onset of action than SSRIs. Dropout rates were similar between mirtazapine and other antidepressants, but its side effect profile was distinct.
